lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: Big Questions from Bear Island
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 1, Session 1
lesson.footer: Persuasive Writing | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 1 Session 1
lesson.fileName: Session 1 - Big Questions from Bear Island.pptx

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LA02 moving beyond bare assertions by taking account of differing opinions; VC2E5LY01 present and justify an opinion; VC2E5LE02 form and share opinions on a literary text (The Last Bear)
plan.shape: sort then make: students sort facts from issues at speed, then turn the novel's big ideas into their own arguable questions, because choosing a real issue is what makes them want to write this term
plan.criticalFeature: an issue is a question fair people could disagree on, not a fact you can look up
decisionPoints: the choice check: which is the best issue to argue?
the exit board: a new topic turned into an issue
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Today is Claim it: pick a side of a real issue.
plan.catchUp: First session of the unit, no catch-up needed. A student who misses it starts tomorrow with the Supported Worksheet.

studentTools: The class copy of The Last Bear by Hannah Gold
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
boardSetup: Four corner signs around the room: Strongly agree, Agree, Disagree, Strongly disagree
A class Issues Wall: a strip of butcher's paper headed Big Questions from Bear Island

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: fact or issue, make an issue, find the mistake, then claim your own big question.
resources.title: Big Questions
resources.subtitle: Facts, issues and your own big question.

example.prompt: Is this a fact or an issue? Polar bears have black skin under their fur.
example.answer: Fact. You can look it up, and nobody can fairly disagree.

items.prompt: Sort the cards: FACT or ISSUE.
cards: Should people kayak near polar bears?
Sea ice is frozen sea water.
Is it fair to keep whales in aquariums?
Should kids be paid for chores?

FACT: Sea ice is frozen sea water.
ISSUE: Should people kayak near polar bears?
Is it fair to keep whales in aquariums?
Should kids be paid for chores?

example.prompt: Big idea: litter at the beach.
steps: Could a fair person say no?
example.answer: Should people be fined for littering at the beach?

items.prompt: Turn each big idea into a should-question.
answers: Should supermarkets stop selling plastic bags?
Should people be allowed to keep wild animals as pets?
Should families drive less to slow the melting ice?
Should kids have a daily screen time limit?

example.prompt: Which is a real issue? A: How big is a polar bear? B: Should zoos keep polar bears?
steps: Test A: can I look it up?
example.answer: B, because fair people could say yes or no.

items.prompt: Which is the best issue to write about?
options: Should countries protect polar bears more?
items.explain: The middle one: people could argue yes or no. The first is a fact; the last is a feeling.

items.prompt: Ben wrote this as his issue. Find his mistake and fix it.
work: My issue: How many polar bears live in Canada?
items.answer: It is a fact you can look up. Fix: Should Canada do more to protect its polar bears?

example.prompt: Issue: Should zoos keep polar bears?
example.answer: I believe zoos should not keep polar bears because they need huge spaces, cold and freedom.

items.prompt: Write your own big question from The Last Bear. Claim your side, then give three reasons.
items.answer: A should-question, a clear claim (I believe...) and three different reasons.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: the best reason on each side, and a fair question that does not pick a side.
resources.title: Both Sides
resources.subtitle: Strong writers know the other side's best reason.

example.answer: YES: zoos pay for research. NO: bears need huge spaces. NO is stronger: research can happen in the wild.

items.prompt: Write the strongest reason for each side.
rows: Should people live on Bear Island?
Should tourists see polar bears up close?
Should kids keep a secret to protect a friend?
answers: Should people live on Bear Island?
The bears need it to themselves
Should tourists see polar bears up close?
Should kids keep a secret to protect a friend?
Adults may need to know to keep them safe

example.prompt: Which question is fair? A: Should mean councils ban dogs? B: Should councils ban dogs from beaches?
steps: Look for words that pick a side

items.prompt: Which question is fairer to both sides?
options: Should cruel zoos be shut down?
items.explain: The second. 'Cruel' already picks a side, so the question isn't fair.

items.prompt: Write a fair issue question about the Arctic. Then write one word that would make it unfair.
items.answer: e.g. Should ships sail through Arctic waters? Unfair word: greedy.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: Supported option: the same task with picture clues, a first answer done and sentence frames.
resources.title: Big Questions Helper
resources.subtitle: A question people argue about is an issue.

example.prompt: Circle the issue: A: Snow is cold. B: Should snow days close schools?

items.hint: An issue is a question people argue about.

options: Should we protect the sea ice?
items.hint: Could a fair person say no?

example.prompt: Big idea: dogs at the beach.
example.answer: Should dogs be allowed on the beach?

rows: Should shops stop selling plastic bags?
answers: Should shops stop selling plastic bags?
items.hint: The first one is done for you.

example.answer: I believe zoos should not keep polar bears because they need space.

items.prompt: Choose one question above. Finish the frame: I believe ___ should ___ because ___.
items.hint: Choose the question you care about most.
Who else would agree with you?

slides.notes: Open the unit. One line: this term we stop learning about persuasive writing and start doing it, for real causes.

slides.title: For the teacher: Weeks 1-5 at a glance
lines: Weeks 1-5: students apply the persuasive structure they know. Final piece: a published persuasive text on an issue from The Last Bear.
This week: find issues, take a position, see other perspectives, debate.
Today: fact or issue, then each student chooses their own big question.
Unit anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. (flag, magnifier, megaphone)
Writing every session: a quick write plus a sustained You Do in writing books.
slides.notes: Teacher-facing only. Skip it in front of the class. The structure students already know (introduction, body paragraphs, conclusion) is applied, not re-taught.

Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for students who need a first step (about one in five). Put the four corner signs up before the session.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to turn a big idea from The Last Bear into a question worth arguing about.
successCriteria: I can tell a fact from an issue.
I can write a should-question from the novel that fair people could disagree on.
I can take a side and give three reasons that would convince someone else.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Today we find the big questions hiding inside our novel.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Spotting a fact is where everyone starts.
Writing your own big question is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 fact or issue is reachable for all; SC2 writing an arguable should-question is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 three convincing reasons is the stretch.

slides.title: Thumbs up, down or sideways?
lines: Polar bears live in the Arctic.
Kids should get a vote in elections.

notes.answer: the middle one is a fact: nobody can disagree, so there is nothing to argue
beats: SAY: Three statements. Show me what you think of each one.
No talking, just thumbs.
ASK: Homework should be banned. Thumbs up, down or sideways?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: a mix. Repeat for the other two.
ASK: Which one was strange to vote on? Why?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: the polar bear one, it's just true
SAY: Last term you wrote opinions with reasons.
This term we write about things that really matter.
And it starts with finding something worth arguing about.
trap: saying the polar bear one is an opinion because people like bears.
Fix: ask could a fair person say no? Student checks with the atlas fact.
notes.prep: Launch bridges Term 3 persuasive writing (opinion plus reasons) to choosing a real issue. Brisk, 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: A question that fair people could disagree about.
slides.example: Should zoos keep polar bears? Some say yes, some say no.

notes.answer: a question fair people could disagree about
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Issue. Say it with me. Issue.
SAY: An issue is a question that fair, sensible people could disagree about.
The scales show it: there's weight on both sides.
ASK: Is 'What colour is a polar bear?' an issue? Why not?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: no, you can look it up, nobody disagrees
trap: thinking any question is an issue.
Fix: ask could a fair person argue the other side? Student tests it.
notes.prep: The word the unit runs on. The test is said here first: could a fair person disagree?

slides.title: From big idea to big question
lines: Big idea: the sea ice is melting.
Fact question: Is the sea ice melting? (look it up)
Issue: Should people fly less to protect the sea ice? (argue it)

notes.answer: the issue is the should-question, because fair people could say yes or no
beats: POINT to the big idea.
SAY: In The Last Bear, the sea ice is melting.
That's a big idea.
POINT to the fact question.
SAY: Is the ice melting? Scientists can measure that.
It's a fact. Nothing to argue.
POINT to the issue.
SAY: But should people fly less to protect it?
Some say yes. Some say flights matter too. Now we've got an issue.
ASK: What word did I start the issue with?
5 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: should
trap: writing a question that has one right answer.
Fix: student says the opposite answer aloud; if it sounds silly, rewrite.
notes.stretch: Make a second issue from the same big idea.
notes.help: Start from the stem: Should people...
notes.prep: The model. Critical feature: an issue is a question fair people could disagree on, not a fact. Near-miss shown side by side.

slides.title: Fact or issue?
slides.pivot: say the opposite aloud: could a fair person believe it?
slides.followUp: cold call one student: how did you know?

items.text: Polar bears hunt seals on the sea ice.
Should tourists be allowed to visit polar bear areas?
How many polar bears are left in the world?
items.answer: 1 - fact. It's a question, but you can look it up
items.say: Fact. It's a question, but scientists can count. Tick or fix.

items.text: Is it right to feed a hungry wild animal?
items.answer: 2 - issue. No should, but people disagree
items.say: Issue. No should, but fair people disagree. Tick or fix.

items.text: Arctic sea ice is smaller in summer than in winter.
Should children help make decisions about the environment?

say: One finger for a fact. Two fingers for an issue.
trap: Fix: ask can we look it up? Student re-sorts.
notes.stretch: Turn each fact into an issue.
notes.help: Ask: could someone say no and still be fair?
notes.prep: Guided sort with the near-misses: a fact in question form, an issue with no should. SC1.

slides.title: Which is the best issue to argue?

options.misconception: picks a fact you can look up on a map

options.text: Should people be allowed to live on Bear Island?

options.misconception: picks a feeling, not a question others could argue

notes.answer: B - should people be allowed to live on Bear Island?
beats: SAY: Three choices. Only one is a real issue.
ASK: Which is the best issue to argue?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: give me one reason someone might say no.
Less -> run the fair-person test on each, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. Some people say yes, for science. Others say leave it to the animals.
trap: pointing to C because it's an opinion.
Fix: ask what would the other side say? Student hears there is no other side.
notes.prep: First decision point, on new items. Under 80% means a second run of the fact-or-issue test before students write.

slides.title: Turn the big idea into an issue
slides.pivot: build one together from the stem Should people...
slides.followUp: cold call two boards: would a fair person say no?

items.text: Big idea: rubbish in the ocean
items.expect: a should-question, e.g. Should plastic bags be banned?

items.text: Big idea: wild animals in zoos
items.expect: e.g. Should zoos keep large wild animals?

items.text: Big idea: keeping secrets from adults
items.answer: Should kids ever keep a secret to protect someone?
items.expect: e.g. Is it ever right to keep a secret from a parent?

items.text: Big idea: people and wild animals as friends
items.answer: Should people try to make friends with wild animals?
items.expect: e.g. Should people go near wild animals?

say: Each big idea comes from our novel. Write a question people could argue about.
trap: writing a fact question, like Are zoos big?
Fix: student adds Should, then tests: could a fair person say no?
notes.stretch: Write the question so that both sides sound reasonable.
notes.help: Copy the stem Should people... then finish it.
notes.prep: Guided making. Big ideas link to the novel without needing a passage. SC2.

slides.title: Four corners: Claim it!
lines: Should humans be allowed to live on Bear Island?
Go to your corner. Convince someone from another corner in 30 seconds.

notes.answer: open - any side, with a reason
beats: POINT to the flag.
SAY: Every piece this term runs on three moves. Claim it. Prove it. Sell it.
Today we claim it.
ASK: Should humans be allowed to live on Bear Island? Decide.
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to your corner... now.
EXPECT: every arm pointing. Then everyone walks there.
ASK: Find someone from another corner. Give them your best reason.
30 sec each. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: scientists need the island; the bears need it more
SAY: Did anyone's reason pull someone across? That's what a good reason does.
trap: repeating the claim as the reason.
Fix: ask why? once more, student adds a because.
notes.stretch: Use your opponent's reason in your reply.
notes.help: Start with: I think yes because... or I think no because...
notes.prep: Movement break and oral rehearsal before writing. Introduces the unit anchor. 5 minutes.

slides.title: Write your Issue Card
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet: sort, make issues, spot the problem, then claim your own big question.

beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Now it's yours. Choose a question you actually care about.
That's the one you'll write best.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Read the question first: could a fair person say no?
TIME 12 minutes.
At 8 minutes, two students read their question for the Issues Wall.
trap: three reasons that say the same thing.
Fix: ask who each reason would convince, student swaps one out.
notes.stretch: Extension: the best reason on both sides, and a fair question.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: picture clues, a first answer done, sentence frames.
notes.prep: Independent application. The Issue Card is the seed for the week and is reused on Thursday's debate. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in the student's own should-question, claim and three reasons

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: New topic: mobile phones at school. Turn it into an issue people would argue over.
Which side are you on? Write one sentence.

notes.answer: e.g. Should mobile phones be banned at school? Claim with a side
beats: SAY: A brand new topic. Show me you can make it into an issue.
ASK: Write an issue question about phones at school, then your side.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: Should phones be banned at school? I believe they should because...
RECORD who writes a fact question, like How many kids have phones? Tomorrow's small group.
trap: writing a fact question about phones.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a topic no slide used. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Tell your partner your big question and the reason most likely to change someone's mind.

notes.answer: open - listen for a real should-question and a reason that names who it convinces
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can turn a big idea into an issue?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
A thumb up with a fact question on the board matters most.
ASK: Tell your partner your big question and your strongest reason.
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: Should zoos keep polar bears? No, because they walk huge distances
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. Tomorrow's small group comes from both. SC2.
